messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 19
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Unemployed
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 61

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory/Mechanical: Motorcycle noise, Auditory (Language): Shouting in Arabic, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Anniversaries: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event, Avoid Night: Going out at night or being outside after dark, Avoid Own Body: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

Vignette:
Asmaa's life had been on hold for nearly two years, ever since the night she was assaulted by a stranger while walking home from a friend's house. She was 17 at the time, and her parents had just received news that they would be moving to the United States from their native Iraq. The stress of the upcoming move, combined with the trauma of the assault, left Asmaa feeling like she was living in a state of suspended animation. The memories of that night were still raw and vivid for Asmaa. She remembered the sound of motorcycle engines roaring down the street as her attacker approached her. The smell of alcohol on his breath made her stomach turn to this day. And when someone shouted at her in Arabic, she was instantly transported back to that moment. It didn't matter if it was a passing stranger or a family member trying to get her attention - the sound sent a jolt of fear through her body. Asmaa's life had become increasingly restricted as she tried to avoid triggers that might bring on these flashbacks. She stopped going out at night, afraid of being outside after dark. She avoided anniversaries and dates connected to the event, fearing that the memories would come flooding back. Even simple things like taking a shower or getting dressed made her anxious - she couldn't bear to look at her own body, which felt like it had been irreparably damaged. Her husband, Ali, tried to be supportive, but Asmaa's withdrawal from life was starting to take a toll on their relationship. He would try to encourage her to go out with him, or engage in activities she used to enjoy, but Asmaa just couldn't shake the feeling that she was no longer capable of doing the things that defined her. She had always been an outgoing person, loved by her friends and family for her bright smile and infectious laugh. But now, she felt like a shadow of her former self. Asmaa's days were filled with hypervigilance - constantly listening for sounds that might indicate someone was entering her home, frequently looking over her shoulder to check if someone was following her. She would catch herself frozen in place, reliving the moments leading up to the assault as if it were happening all over again. Her memories of that night were fragmented and sensory - she could smell the alcohol on her attacker's breath, hear the sound of his voice shouting at her in Arabic. It was as if her mind had stored these details away, waiting for some unsuspecting trigger to set them off once more. Asmaa's assault had shattered her beliefs about how the world worked. She used to think that bad things only happened to bad people, or that there was always someone who would step in to stop something terrible from happening. But now, she knew that wasn't true - and it left her feeling lost and vulnerable. She couldn't help but wonder if she had somehow brought this upon herself, or if someone else would have been able to stop the attack. Asmaa's life was at a standstill, waiting for some sign of hope or redemption. But until then, she felt trapped in a cycle of fear and avoidance, unable to shake the memories that haunted her every waking moment.
